**Question:** When `create` runs into a file or subdirectory it isn't allowed to read inside a directory you asked it to archive, should the tool detect that before it starts writing — leaving no archive file behind at all — or is it allowed to discover the problem partway through and leave an incomplete archive? (FR-016 / FR-021)

**Why it matters:** User Story 3 promises that a failed `create` is indistinguishable from never having run it, but FR-021 allows an incomplete archive to survive a read failure. Those two can't both be true for an unreadable nested file, and the answer decides whether the tool walks your folders once or twice — and what the test for this case is allowed to assert.

**Recommended:** Option A - The spec's whole safety story is "validate everything before writing anything", and an unreadable entry *is* something the tool can check up front. It also mirrors the plan-then-write structure `extract` already uses, so there's no new machinery, and re-walking 10,000 small files stays far inside the 10-second budget in SC-010.

| Option | Description |
|--------|-------------|
| A | Walk every named path fully before writing, confirming each file and directory can actually be opened for reading. An unreadable entry means exit 2 with no archive created. An incomplete archive then only ever results from a genuine mid-write surprise such as a full disk. |
| B | Check only the paths the user typed (they exist, they're safe). Unreadable entries deeper in the tree surface while writing, so the run exits 2 and may leave an incomplete archive, exactly as FR-021 permits. |
| C | Walk every named path before writing to record what's there and what type it is, but don't test read permission. Read failures surface mid-write and may leave an incomplete archive. |
| Short | Provide a different short answer (≤5 words) |

You can reply with the option letter (e.g., "A"), accept the recommendation by saying "yes" or "recommended", or provide your own short answer.
